Mr. Speaker, after having carefully considered the resolution of the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise), we come to the conclusion that it is of course a bill which reflects a magnanimity which is all to the honour of the mover.
Nobody wishes to cast any doubt on the generosity of his intention. I think such a proposal deserves to be seriously examined, but there is a long way to go before we proceed to pass such a bill. There are provisions of the budget which must be considered before we can say whether this proposal can be immediately approved.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
It is a good idea to point out in passing, without introducing political partisanship in this debate, that our good friends of the Ralliement des Creditistes are those who advocate most vigourously at all times that

taxes must be cut and even abolished if possible. But, on the other hand, they are the first to propose measures sometimes expensive, and prohibitive, and those who are responsible for the government feel a certain regret, a certain nostalgia, because if one day-I cannot see that it will happen-we were in opposition-I repeat that it will not happen-we would be so happy to harass the government with all kinds of requests.
You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that if, 25 or 30 years from now, circumstances have us in the opposition, we will be the first to beg, to show great generosity, to ask the government without cease to do more for the pensioners and to ease as much as possible the taxpayers' burden. Then also, 30 or 35 years from now, the gentlemen opposite will say: Live up to your responsibilities, be serious, analyse the funds available in the budget, to see whether or not we can afford to make such outlandish promises, to launch out on such costly ventures that they could lead to the bankruptcy of the government.
Mr. Speaker, a very summary analysis of public accounts shows that for pensions, veterans allowances, family allowances, allowances to disabled and blind persons, etc., the government spends $3,350,000 for the disabled and blind persons allowances, and, according to the estimates for 1967-68, $15 million will be paid to the disabled and family allowance payments will reach $610 million.
I wish to bring to the attention of our Creditiste friends, who were shouting across Quebec the slogan:	"Double our family
allowances", that this would require an expenditure of $610 million for the government and that they have never suggested where such a tremendous amount would come from, in order to pay the cost of ridiculous promises.
Concerning old age security, my hon friend and colleague, the member for Labelle (Mr. Clermont), has clearly indicated for the year 1967-1968 an estimated expenditure of about $1,400 million.
Mr. Speaker, if that does not show how the government is concerned with social security, I wonder what should be done to convince our people that no other government has ever demonstrated such concern for the security of our Canadian population.
As I said a while ago, I believe the steps suggested by our hon friend, the member for Chapleau, to be most generous in spirit but
November 1, 1967

rather difficult to enact in terms of the budget. Of course, the miraculous and key solution which has always been advocated by our friends of the Ralliement Creditiste, is the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada is the answer to unemployment.
One day, I asked the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste, the hon. member for Vil-leneuve (Mr. Caouette), who is a dear friend of mine, and a very good, eager and stirring speaker, what would happen to unemployment if, some day, the Social Credit theory were put into practise, and he replied that unemployment would completely disappear in the province of Quebec. I am glad that the leader of the Ralliement Creditiste can delight in such imaginary situations, but I do not think there are, in the world, a great many economists who could accept that theory, namely that once the Ralliement Creditiste would be in power, unemployment would disappear completely and forever.
But there are people who like to dream, who delight in utopia and day-dreams. So let us not disturb them, Mr. Speaker.
So, what is the solution for all those problems? The Bank of Canada: solution for unemployment; the Bank of Canada: solution for governments' debts; the Bank of Canada: solution for individual debts; the Bank of Canada: solution for inadequate productivity; the Bank of Canada: solution for the sterility of women; the Bank of Canada: solution for everybody's problems.
As for us, we are much more realistic and cautious and I must say that some of the theories set forth, namely that in wartime, the required money is found, whereas in peacetime, it is not found, are terrible fallacies. If money is found in wartime, it is because the government borrows it; it borrows because it is an emergency.
Mr. Speaker, I understand the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe): we admire him for fighting in this house and for waging war on poverty. I might tell him that the first to conceive the wonderful idea of waging war on poverty was a representative on the government side, and the slogan of war on poverty was invented by a member on this side of the house. The government appropriated this idea in a recent speech from the throne, in 1965. The government started an anti-poverty program.
We are also extremely interested in this program which could be not only speeded up but intensified as much as possible in order to eliminate poverty. We are also conscious
Old Age Security Act of that problem. However, instead of advocating senseless theories, we remain with the issue, which is to say that we are realistically considering the solutions necessary.
All the measures introduced by the government are certainly meant, one way or the other, to fight poverty, and it is with pride that we, members of the party in power, can say that the whole social legislation of Canada is the work, the exclusive work of the Liberal party.
Mr. Speaker, one could make witty remarks about the hon. member's motion. I wonder whether this would not be a means of encouraging middle-age urge. Some old men are on the look-out for young blond girls, because they know that at 70 or 75, besides receiving a pension, they will be able to double their pension if they find an attractive young wife. That would be encouraging middle-age urge and it would be unwholesome.
But to speak in a more serious vein, let us say that in addition to all the expenditures made by the government in the field of social security, if the measure proposed by the hon. member were passed immediately, the following expenditures would have to be incurred in the following order. First of all, it would be necessary to institute a full inquiry to determine the exact number of married men entitled to old age pension benefits and that of the men whose wives are younger and not entitled to those benefits. According to a rough estimate, I think that such an expenditure would total $150 million. Moreover-there I come to the idea of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) whose answer is this. The widows of the same age, that is those who are not yet entitled to old age security benefits but who are of the same age as the wives of those who are entitled to them, would have to be granted that pension according to the same principle. This would mean an expenditure of about $140 million added to the expenditure I have mentioned of $150 million for a total of $290 million.

Can the hon. member tell us exactly what budget expenditures will have to be cut to find these $340 million. If the hon. member, for instance, who is entitled to post offices this year in his constituency, were to tell us that he does not want those post offices but that the money should be earmarked for the spouse of those entitled to old age pension, that they should be given this money, that the post offices would be cut off, then we are all for it. Let him tell us whether he wants to give up his salary and we will be very happy to oblige.
As far as I am concerned, I would be highly in favour of cutting the hon. member's salary. That does not affect me, Mr. Speaker, but it might affect others, because when one has no money, it does not change anything to have less, because one has none at all. Perhaps the hon. member is a rich man; I do not know whether he would accept to have his salary reduced, but I say to him that, personally, I look with favour upon the reduction of hon. members' pay.
I am very frank with the hon. member, Mr. Speaker. The leader of the Ralliement Creditiste was the first to say, on a television program broadcast throughout the province, that $18,000 was too high a salary for members. I wonder when the member gave up part of his indemnity, gave it to charity.
All this to say that demagoguery is easy, that it is easy to say that members receive too high a salary, that farmers are not as well paid. Still, when the time comes for action, we see that those who preach great principles with ardour show far less sincerity in applying them.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say the member has a very generous idea, which deserves to be studied with care, but those who are responsible for the administration are entitled to make what normal objections come up from the point of view of practical application, of budgetary economic realities. Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to second the motion of the hon. member for Chap-leau (Mr. Laprise). This motion is rightly called for, in my estimation, because we must ask that a pension be paid to those people who do not receive any, because, under the present system that governs us, credit and full income have been taken away from the people through taxation and assessment, also through unemployment caused, in fact, by the system applied by the hon. members on the other side.
Unemployment was rife for 1G, 15 years, for decades, then was followed by the war. After all that, an extreme burden was placed on everyone through various taxes and assessments. Taxpayers saw their whole income taken away from them, and the reason why everyone is penniless and clamours for wage increases, it is that people are no longer able to live, having been fleeced by previous administrations. The Liberals are in power-and when the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Choquette) says that it feels good to be with the opposition-well, if it feels that good, I suggest that he resign and come with the opposition. It is easier to be with the opposition? The way things are, nothing can be done. He says that there is nothing for him to do on the government side, and that anything can be done on the side of the opposition? Well, he should come with his wise suggestions to the opposition side.
I do not know what is wrong with him, but anyhow he says there is nothing he can do about the economic situation, to find funds. The Creditistes are talking about the Bank of Canada, he says, but would it not be better to lend money interest free through the Bank of Canada to finance public goods, instead of merely encouraging the big concerns and the big financiers, whose profits amount to billions every year?
I could name institutions which have billions in revenue every year but which pay nevertheless about a quarter of the taxes paid by the small taxpayer. At this time and in the present system-not the Social Credit system-the little people are the ones who pay taxes. The big shots are given the right to all sorts of reserve funds: hidden reserves, direct reserves, indirect reserves. They also enjoy the right to every kind of depreciation. The tax schedule is terribly unfair.
November 1, 1967

There are great injustices, but the hon. member does not mention them. It he wanted to be honest, he would simply tell us: the money is not to be found. Then, I would answer him: Think about the $18 billion surplus that has been capitalized this year and will amount to $22 billion in 1967-68. It is possible in some places to find a few millions in order to enable certain people to live decently. Under our present system, we would not have to tax everybody in general, to keep on accumulating debts, to increase the budget, to go deep into debt and to have a deficit of over $1 billion this year.
We have had deficits since the end of the war. The member for Lotbiniere tells us that it is all right to borrow money in wartime and to spend it. But we should do the same in peacetime. If it is permissible to live in times of war, while killing our fellow-men, it should be all the more so in times of peace when it is the right time to live. When the time comes to live, all we are given is taxes and more taxes.
When old age pensions are increased, taxes are increased also by about one and one-half times what is needed for those pensions, because the coffers of the government must be filled and deficits reduced.
When there is a deficit, when the administration is always financed by taxes, when no solution is found to manage and promote the economy, at least you should have the courtesy of not laughing at those who have found solutions and who can prove it with figures in black and white. I can erase Canada's debt within ten years and reduce taxes by 50 per cent. Is that enough for the hon. member? Can he find such solutions himself? No, but he finds that ridiculous. The present debt is ridiculous and the present taxes are also ridiculous.
Since I do not want to kill this motion, I conclude by saying that I strongly support it. I commend its sponsor and ask that the question be put.
